EAQ84.brief: Lumen does not light the real scene directly. It builds a simpler copy called the Lumen Scene, and it stores the look of each surface in a Surface Cache. When a mesh is missing from this cache, it shows as pink in the debug view, and the bounced light around it looks wrong. In this quest you use the Lumen view modes to find those pink areas in a level and fix one of them.
checklist: Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Open an interior level of your own that has Lumen turned on, or build a small room from cubes and fill it with props from the Starter Content, including some with complex shapes such as chairs and shelves. Open View Mode, then Lumen, then Surface Cache. Take a screenshot and circle every pink area on it.

Open one pink prop (an SM_ mesh) in the Static Mesh Editor. If nothing is pink, pick the prop with the most complex shape. In Build Settings, raise Max Lumen Mesh Cards from 12 to 24 and click Apply Changes. Then check the Surface Cache view again.
In the console, run r.Lumen.Visualize.CardPlacement 1 and look at the cards on that mesh. Cards are the flat pieces Lumen uses to capture a surface. Set the value back to 0.

Open Show, then Visualize, then Mesh DistanceFields. Find one thin wall or window mesh that looks like a soft blob. In its Build Settings, set Distance Field Resolution Scale to 2.0 and click Apply Changes. Compare the result.

Place a Post Process Volume with Infinite Extent (Unbound) turned on, or use the one in your level. In it, set Lumen Scene View Distance to a small value and look at a far corner. Then set it back to the default.
Open Show, then Lumen, and untick Screen Traces. Take a screenshot of the same view with Screen Traces and without them.

Open Project Settings, then Engine, then Rendering. Write down whether Support Hardware Ray Tracing and Use Hardware Ray Tracing when available are turned on, and which Software Ray Tracing Mode is set.

Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Open a level that has a Directional Light, some static props, a few foliage meshes with a wind material (one that uses World Position Offset), and one large building mesh without Nanite. To build it quickly: place props from the Starter Content, place a few bushes and give them a material in which a Sine of a Time node, multiplied by a small vector, is connected to World Position Offset, and scale a cube into a large building block.

Open View Modes, then Virtual Shadow Map, then Cached Page. Keep the camera still and take a screenshot. Red pages that appear while the camera is still are cache invalidations, which means cached pages were thrown away.
Switch to the Shadow Casters visualization and find which objects cause the red pages. Check that their bounds, the invisible boxes around them, are not much bigger than the meshes.

Select the foliage meshes. In the Details panel, set Shadow Cache Invalidation Behavior to Rigid and check the Cached Page view again. Then set World Position Offset Disable Distance to a distance where you can no longer see the wind.

In the console, run r.ShaderPrintEnable 1 and then r.Shadow.Virtual.Stats 1. Write down the values Allocated, Cached and Invalidated. Rotate the Directional Light a little and watch Invalidated jump up.
Enable Nanite on the large building mesh. Move the camera slowly and compare the stats and the Cached Page view with before.
Write three lines: what caused most of the invalidations, what you changed, and what you would never do to a Directional Light while the game runs.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open Project Settings, then Engine, then Rendering, and find the Direct Lighting section. Enable MegaLights, and accept the prompt that asks to enable Support Hardware Ray Tracing. Restart the editor.

In a new level, build a dark hall from cubes with a floor, walls and pillars. Place at least 20 Movable local lights: Point Lights, Spot Lights, and 2 Rect Lights with a Source Texture (any texture works). Turn Cast Shadows on for all of them.
Add a Post Process Volume with Infinite Extent turned on. Use its MegaLights setting to turn MegaLights off, and read the number from stat GPU. Then turn MegaLights on again and compare the number.
Open View Modes, then MegaLights, then Light Complexity. Move the mouse over a wall between many lights, and take a screenshot of the list of lights and their weight ratios.
Find one light that is partly inside a wall or reaches very far. Make its Source Width, Source Height, cone angle or Attenuation Radius smaller until it no longer shines through geometry.
On one Spot Light, set MegaLights Shadow Method to Virtual Shadow Maps. Compare the shadow detail on a Nanite prop with the shadow from a Ray Tracing light next to it.

Open one prop in the Static Mesh Editor. Under Nanite Settings, set Fallback Target to Fallback Relative Error (some versions show this option as Relative Error), lower the Fallback Relative Error value, and click Apply Changes. See if its shadow gets more accurate.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Download one free IES profile from the website of a lighting manufacturer. The documentation page linked on this quest names Lithonia and Philips. Import it with the Add button of the Content Browser, or drag and drop the file.
Open the imported IES asset in the Texture Editor. Write down its Brightness, which is given in candelas, and the read-only value Texture Multiplier.

Build a dark room from cubes in a new level. Place a Point Light, a Spot Light and a Rect Light on the same wall. Under Light Profiles, assign the same IES Texture to each of them. Take a screenshot of all three.
Set the Outer Cone Angle of the Spot Light to 30, and then to 80. Watch where the profile is cut off.
On the Point Light, enable Use IES Intensity. Try IES Intensity Scale at 1.0 and at 0.25. Then disable Use IES Intensity and compare with the light's own Intensity.
In the Texture Editor, set Brightness to 0 and save. Look at the Point Light with Use IES Intensity turned on. Put the original value back afterwards.
Make one Light Function material that imitates the same shape and put it on a fourth light. Note in one line which is the cheaper way to shape a light.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Start from a level that has a Directional Light with Atmosphere Sun Light turned on, a Sky Atmosphere, and a Sky Light with Real Time Capture turned on. A new Basic level has these actors, and you can add missing ones with the Env. Light Mixer. Open Window > Env. Light Mixer and use it to add a Volumetric Cloud if the level has none.

In the Content Browser, enable Show Engine Content and find the folder Engine/EngineSky/VolumetricClouds. Make a Material Instance of the cloud material in your own Content folder, and name it MI_Clouds_01. Assign it to the Volumetric Cloud component.
In MI_Clouds_01, change Layout_GlobalCoverage, the Layout_CloudType channels and Cloud_GlobalDensity until you have a sky that is partly cloudy. Add a little wind with Layout_WindControls.

On the Directional Light, enable Cast Cloud Shadows. Try a small and a large Cloud Shadow Extent, and try Cloud Shadow Map Resolution Scale at 0.5 and at 2. Take a screenshot of the cloud shadows on the ground.
On the Sky Light, open Atmosphere and Cloud and raise the strength of Cloud Ambient Occlusion. Compare how the bottoms of the clouds look.

In the console, try r.VolumetricRenderTarget.Mode 0, 1 and 2 while you fly near a tall mesh that reaches into the cloud layer. Note which mode does not cut into the mesh. Then set it back to the default.
Turn Storm_Clouds up in MI_Clouds_01 and take one screenshot of the storm look.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open an outdoor level that has a low area, or create a new level with a Landscape and sculpt a valley. Place an Exponential Height Fog, enable Volumetric Fog on it, and keep the Fog Density low. Give the Directional Light a Volumetric Scattering Intensity of 1.

Create a material named M_FogSphere and set Material Domain to Volume. Make a SphereMask that compares Absolute World Position with Particle Position and takes its radius from Particle Radius. Multiply it by a tiling noise texture, for example a noise or cloud texture from the engine content, or by a Noise node, and connect the result to Extinction. Connect a constant 1 to Albedo.
Create a simple Niagara sprite system named FXS_LowFog with a few large, slow particles. Assign M_FogSphere in its Sprite Renderer. Place the system in the low area.
Save a camera bookmark. Take a screenshot of the valley with FXS_LowFog hidden and another with it visible, both from that same bookmark.
Place a Spot Light in the fog. Turn Cast Volumetric Shadow off and on, and read stat GPU or profilegpu for both cases.
Set Scattering Distribution on the fog to 0.9. Look toward the sun and then away from it. Then set it back to the default.
Add a light that flickers, driven by a Blueprint or by Sequencer. If it leaves trails in the fog, set its Volumetric Scattering Intensity to 0.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Pick a small level with a Directional Light, a Sky Light, a few local lights and some props. If you have none, build a small room scene from cubes and Starter Content props in a new Basic level and add two Point Lights. Duplicate the level and name the copy L_Bake_01. Set the Directional Light and the Sky Light to Stationary, and the local lights to Static. Open Project Settings, then Rendering, and check that Allow Static Lighting is on.

Open Edit > Plugins, go to Built-In, then Editor, and enable GPU Lightmass. Before you restart, open Project Settings and enable Support Hardware Ray Tracing, Enable Virtual Texture Support and Enable Virtual Texture Lightmaps. Under Platforms, then Windows, set Default RHI to DirectX 12. Then restart.
Open Build > GPU Lightmass. Pick Bake What You See, keep the viewport in Realtime, and click Build Lighting. Move a prop while it bakes and watch the tiles update. Click Save, and then Cancel.
Now choose Full Bake. Turn Realtime off in the viewport with Ctrl+R and click Build Lighting. Write down how long it took.
Find one prop whose shadows look blotchy. Raise its Lightmap Resolution in the Details panel, bake again, and compare.
Take a screenshot of the baked level and one of the Lumen version from the same view. Write two lines on what each one does better.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open a level that has a dark interior and a door to a bright exterior, or build a closed box from cubes with one open door in a new Basic level. Place a Post Process Volume with Infinite Extent (Unbound) turned on as the global volume, if the level has none, and set its Metering Mode to Auto Exposure Histogram.
Open Project Settings, then Rendering, then Default Settings, and enable Extend default luminance range in Auto Exposure settings. Note that Min Brightness and Max Brightness are now shown in EV100.
Turn on Show > Visualize > HDR (Eye Adaptation). Stand outside and then inside, and write down the Average Scene EV100 for both places.

Create a Curve Float asset named CF_ExposureComp (click Add, then Miscellaneous, then Curve). Add a key at your outdoor EV100 with the value -0.5, and a key at your indoor EV100 with the value +0.5. Assign the asset to Exposure Compensation Curve, and watch Exposure Compensation (Curve) change as you walk.

Make a small grayscale texture named T_MeteringMask that is bright in the center and dark at the edges. Assign it to Exposure Metering Mask. Look at the bright door from the side, so that it sits at the edge of the screen, and compare how stable the exposure is.
Open Lens, then Local Exposure, and set Highlight Contrast to 0.8, Shadow Contrast to 0.8 and Blurred Luminance Blend to 0.5. Turn on Show > Visualization > Local Exposure and take a screenshot.
Add a Post Process Volume named PPV_Interior around the room, with Blend Radius 300 and its own Exposure Compensation. Play in the editor, walk through the door and check the transition.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Pick a dense prop with 100k triangles or more, such as a free rock or statue from Fab, Epic's asset store. If you have none, make a dense mesh in Modeling Mode: create a Sphere with a very high subdivision level and accept it as a Static Mesh. Duplicate the mesh and name the copy SM_Fallback_Test. In the Static Mesh Editor, under Nanite Settings, turn on Enable Nanite Support.
In the Static Mesh Editor, press Ctrl + N to switch between the full Nanite mesh and the fallback mesh. Write down the triangle count of each.

Set Fallback Target to Fallback Relative Error (some versions show this option as Relative Error). Try the value 1.0 and then 0.1. Click Apply Changes each time and compare the triangle count of the fallback mesh.
Set Keep Triangle Percent to 50 and Trim Relative Error to 0.05, and click Apply. Compare the Resource Size in the asset details before and after.
Place the prop in a level. In the console, type r.Nanite 0 to see the fallback mesh drawn in the level. Type r.Nanite 1 to go back.
Type NaniteStats in the console and read the information on screen. Then open View Modes, then Nanite Visualization, then Mask. Nanite meshes are green and meshes without Nanite are red.

Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Take a simple prop that has Nanite enabled and one material slot, such as a brick block or a stone slab. A Box made in Modeling Mode with Nanite enabled works. Name it SM_Disp_Test. Get a height (displacement) texture for its surface. A free surface from Fab includes one, and for a first test any grayscale texture works, such as a mask texture from the Starter Content.
Open the prop in the Static Mesh Editor. Under Nanite Settings, set Trim Relative Error to 0.04.
Expand Displacement Maps and add one element (Index 0). Set its Texture to your height map, and set Magnitude to a small value. Start with 2. Click Apply Changes.
Check that Displacement UV Channel matches the UV channel your height map was made for. Then place the prop in a level.
Open View Modes, then Nanite Visualization, then Triangles. Compare the mesh with Magnitude 0 and with your Magnitude.

This step is optional. On a copy of the material, check Enable Tessellation under Nanite in the material Details, connect the height texture to Displacement, and set Magnitude and Center. Compare this tessellation, which happens while the game runs, with the baked result.

Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Collect four props in a test level: a dense scanned rock, a tree made of masked leaf cards, a sky sphere or another big simple mesh, and a modular wall piece that you place 50 times. Free assets from Fab work well. If you have none, use stand-ins: a Sphere with a very high subdivision level from Modeling Mode as the dense rock, the bush from the Starter Content as the tree, a very large sphere as the sky sphere, and a cube scaled into a wall piece.
For each prop, write one line that says Nanite or classic LODs. Give the reason from the Nanite documentation page, such as triangle count, instance count, occluder, VSM shadows or material type.
Enable Nanite on the props you chose. Open View Modes, then Nanite Visualization, then Mask, to confirm which are green (Nanite) and which are red (not Nanite).
Open the Overdraw visualization. Look at the tree and at any kit pieces that are stacked on each other, and note the brightest areas.

Open the rock in the Static Mesh Editor and compare its vertex count with its triangle count. If the vertex count is 2 times the triangle count or more, note that the normals are probably faceted, which means each triangle looks flat.
Type r.Nanite 0 and then r.Nanite 1 in the console, and watch stat unit each time. Add the result to your notes.
